doc.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024

title: Discovering jazz history with Dick Wright at KU
summary: After student teaching he took Dick Wright's jazz history class, switched to Radio/TV/Film and worked in the jazz research library.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: taskmaster. But you would read about the things people had written and a lot of times it just didn’t match up with the person that I had gotten to know. And over the years I would get to know many of those guys on a pretty close level. Because the type of events, the type of things that I was doing kind of required working closely with them, working closely with them on the music, things like that. And then once you can kind of — the other things that I’m proud of is that I had stayed in — you know I was in music at KU long enough, probably about four semesters. I don’t remember when I switched over to Radio/TV/Film, but in the music education side of things they sent us out as freshmen to student teach. And I got sent to a sixth grade string class, of course violins and violas. But you know I had the basic class and you know you have to — and I realized, this isn’t what I want to do at all. I mean I respect it and I know it’s necessary and I was a student, I mean but I didn’t see myself doing that. So luckily they sent you out early enough that you could kind of see if that’s what you wanted or not. So I had been listening for years to KANU, which was the jazz — at night at least — NPR station out of Lawrence, but at night it was jazz and on weekends, and the big, the well-known authority on jazz in the Midwest was Dick Wright. And Dick taught the jazz history classes at KU. And I took that first jazz history class and everything became clear for me. Because I’d read all the books I could find up to that point in the library at high school, but when I took that class I knew a lot of the names, but it all came together. I understood then when I took that class how everything fit together which I didn’t know before. I mean I knew these different people but I didn’t know exactly where they fit within the overall scheme of things, at least not on that level. So when I took that class it opened up everything and I decided at that point to switch to Radio/TV/Film. So I switched majors, started studying, and I went up to Dick one day after class and I said, “You know” I said — I was so shy and I’m still shy actually, I have to not be in certain circumstances but it took a lot for me to go up to him, and I said, “You know I really want to do what you do. I don’t know how to do it but like you know I’d like to play jazz on the radio and I’d like to like teach jazz history because that’s what I really like.” And so I figured dozens of kids had probably gone up to him and said that, but of course no one else had ever said that, he’d been teaching for years. So he kind of took me under his wing and I got to work in the jazz research library there on campus. He had donated 10- 20,000 records at a time when none of those things were available. We’re talking about early ‘80s then. I had access all of a sudden to everything I’d ever dreamed of being able to hear. Not only could I listen to it, I could make cassette copies of anything I wanted, and I had full access to everything. And it changed everything. And then I really delved into the idea of radio, and I really wanted to do the teaching. So for the next two years I immersed myself into that. I even went to summer school so that I could work in the library during the summer

because I mean I just couldn’t wait to get in there and catalogue these things and listen to everything and it just — my education was, you know, quadrupled. But I was a Radio/TV/Film major so I got on the student station and became the jazz program director for a couple of years and was able to start to actually be on the radio and kind of learn how to do that, and of course Dick helped me and so on.
